detail: The evidence-blob verification result is appended to `problems`, but every other diagnostic produced by this routine is accumulated in `notes` — the two adjacent lines (`notes.append("index is stale; ...")` and `notes += _loose_shards(repo)`) show that `notes` is the list this function builds and returns. If `problems` is not part of the value this routine emits (it is not accumulated anywhere else in the visible code), then the new blob check is a silent no-op: given a log whose `gate.failed`/`gate.passed` event names an evidence blob under `.ddflow/blobs/` that has been deleted or altered, `LB.problems(repo, events)` returns the mismatch, it is written into a list that is never surfaced, and `ddflow doctor`/health reports nothing — exactly the scenario the change is supposed to cover ("doctor verifies the blob", acceptance "blob tamper detected by doctor"). The finding is that the message must land in the same list the rest of this routine returns (`notes`, or whatever the caller actually emits), otherwise the tamper check cannot be observed. A failing-first test that tampers with a referenced blob and asserts the message appears in doctor output will fail with the current destination list.

detail: `_prior_evidence` now runs the recorded gate evidence through `LB.full`, which replaces any out-of-line (blob-backed) value with an `Unavailable` sentinel when the referenced blob is absent/tampered. That sentinel is truthy and is not handled here. The sibling paths were all taught to notice it — `_check_triage` (`isinstance(found, B.Unavailable) -> bad("... cannot be triaged until the blob is restored")`), `_merge_delta` (`_hold_unreadable`), and `_context` (`if not found or isinstance(found, B.Unavailable)`) — but the `--chunk` re-review path only does `prior = _prior_evidence(rec)` and then checks `if not prior.get("diff_sha") or "reviewed" not in prior`. Since an `Unavailable` sentinel satisfies `not prior.get("diff_sha") == False` (it is truthy), the "per-chunk evidence is on record" guard passes and the function goes on to build the re-review from the unreadable prior evidence: the prompt/context rendered for the chunk will contain the sentinel (or iterating the prior `chunk_findings`/diff will raise) instead of telling the operator to restore the blob. Concrete input: a clone (or a checkout after blob GC/tamper that `doctor` flags) where a previously recorded `review --chunk` stored its diff tail / findings under `.ddflow/blobs/` and the blob is missing; running `ddflow review ITEM.GATE --chunk N` there is accepted as if the prior review were intact, whereas every other read of the same evidence refuses. `_chunk` needs the same `B.Unavailable` guard the other three call sites got.
title: ddflow/api/review.py:521 (`_chunk`, `_prior_evidence(rec)`)

detail: The knob's own doc admits that with this feature another clone "sees this lease's expiry up to this much earlier than the holder's last heartbeat implies" — i.e. up to `renew_log_min_s` — and claims that skew is "absorbed by ttl_s and grace_s". With the shipped defaults that claim is arithmetically false: `renew_log_min_s` defaults to 300 while `grace_s` defaults to 120, so a clone folding the coalesced log computes `last_written_renewal + ttl_s + grace_s` as reclaimable up to ~180 s earlier than the holder's expectation, and the write-on-threshold rule means the last *written* renewal at the instant of a write can lag the live heartbeat by a further renewal interval. That breaks the intent's requirement that coalescing happen "without changing what an observer on another clone computes as expiry" (and the audit's stated condition for the equivalent local-heartbeat variant: the expiry another clone computes must be unchanged within `grace_s`); a racing clone can reclaim and start editing the same item while the holder still considers itself live. The same default also makes the knob a no-op in the documented configuration: the preceding knob renews a lease every 300 s, so at each renewal the last written renewal is already ≥ the 300 s threshold and every renewal is still written — the acceptance target (lease.renewed under 10% of events) is unreachable. The default needs to sit comfortably *below* `grace_s` (with the fold adjusted so the observer's expiry is unchanged), not at or above the renewal interval and above the grace.
title: ddflow/config_sections/lease.py:25-29 (`renew_log_min_s` default)

detail: The new guard skips `_widen` / `_clashing` / `_join` unless `it.lease_contest` or `it.displaced` is already set, on the stated invariant that "with neither a contest nor a displaced claim on the item there is nothing to widen and nothing to meet". That invariant is circular: `it.lease.renewed_at = at` (line 220) is executed *before* the guard, so `_clashing(_known(it), _claim(it.lease))` compares the already-widened displayed claim (now ending at `at`) against the other claims known for the item — the flags, being pre-existing fold state, were computed against the *unwidened* window. Concretely: item X has lease L (machine A) whose stored window ends at `e`; a committed claim C by machine B on X was folded with start `c > e`, so nothing overlapped at that time and neither `lease_contest` nor `displaced` was ever set for X. A late renewal event for L then arrives with `renewed_at = at` with `c <= at` (a heartbeat replayed after B's claim, exactly the case a `_late_renewal` handler exists for). The old code widened L to `at`, `_clashing` found C, and `_join` merged them, so the folded State marked the pair contested/joined. The new code skips all of it: the overlap exists only *because of* the widening that the guard prevents, so the flags are false and nothing is joined. The folded State (contested groups / lease windows, hence board/status and the expiry another clone computes) therefore differs from the old fold — violating the acceptance requirement of a byte-identical fold on this log. The same skip also leaves the item's stored window un-updated for later events (`_widen` is the only thing that refreshes it here), so a subsequent claim that overlaps the renewed-but-unwidened window is likewise not detected as a contest.
title: ddflow/core/handlers/leases.py:224 (`_late_renewal` guard)

detail: `size` in this method is the byte offset at which the last appended line *starts*, not the shard's new length: the very next statement hands the append hooks `size, size + len(line)` (start, end), and `len(line)` is the just-written line. `ShardMeta.advance` is therefore given the start offset where the design of this change says the sidecar must record a value that can be "verified against the shard sizes/tails" and trusted "past a shard whose size changed". With the start offset recorded, `os.path.getsize(shard)` is always `recorded + len(line)` — it never equals the recorded value even when nothing else has been appended — so on the next `_shard_meta()`/`_stamp_events()` call every shard is treated as changed, the whole shard is re-read, and the sidecar is rewritten again after the next append. Concretely: a fresh process appends one 10-byte event to an empty shard; `advance` records `0` while the shard is 10 bytes, so an immediately following `status`/append in that process (and every later one) is a permanent cache miss, i.e. the "an append does not parse the whole log" optimization is a no-op plus the new sidecar I/O is pure overhead — the acceptance budget (`status` < 2 s, append < 100 ms at 56k events) is not met. (Under the alternative reading where the recorded value is the covered length, the newest event at offset `size` falls outside the covered region and is dropped from the folded facts, so a capability or override first declared by that event never reaches `stamp_facts`/`_judge_skew`.) Either way the recorded value must be the end of the written line, `size + len(line)`, exactly as the hook call beneath it already computes.
title: ddflow/infra/log.py:1098 — `EventLog.append`, `self._meta.advance(self.shard, size, ev)`

detail: The two `stamp_facts(...)` call sites are switched from `self._all_events()` to `self._stamp_events()`. Unless `_stamp_events()` returns exactly the same event set as `_all_events()` (in which case the change would be a no-op and pointless), the strict skew guard now derives its version/format facts from a strictly smaller slice of the log — and unlike the `_highest_lamport` hunk right below it, this path has no fallback to the full scan, so nothing restores coverage. A concrete way this fires: a clone that was offline stamps events with an older release/format and its shard is later merged/rotated into a log whose older shards already carry a newer release's stamps. `_stamp_events()` then yields only the recent window, `stamp_facts` reports no skew, `check_skew(..., strict=True)` passes, and the older binary proceeds to `adopt`/overwrite the newer release's managed text — precisely the case the surrounding docstring says must not happen ("an older ddflow must not overwrite a newer one's") — and to append to a log stamped by a newer version, breaking the acceptance criterion "old ddflow refuses or reads the new log per the skew guard" [D-upgrade-skew-guard]. If the intent really is a cheaper read, the narrowing needs an explicit proof (and a replay-equivalence/old-log test) that every stamped event in every rotated shard is still covered, or a fallback to `_all_events()` when the reduced source cannot be shown complete.
title: ddflow/infra/log.py:1261 (same swap at :1293)

detail:
`ShardMeta.advance` decides whether the in-memory record still describes the shard "as it was just before" using the byte size alone (`row.get("size") != size_before`), while everything else in the module — `_current` at line 67 and the module docstring ("trusts a record only while the shard still has exactly that size and modification time", "…shrunk, **was rewritten** or is new -- sends THAT shard back to a full read") — treats `mtime_ns` as part of the identity of a shard's content.

Concrete failure: `facts()` validates a shard and puts its row in `self._rows`; the shard is then rewritten *in place to the same byte length* before the append's `advance()` call (a repair/upcaster/merge tool rewriting one event line, or a same-length line restored from another clone). `mtime_ns` changed but `size` did not, so line 103 is false, `advance` skips the bail-out, and `_save` writes a record built from the pre-rewrite `row["high"]`/`row["stamps"]` together with the *post-append* `st_size`/`st_mtime_ns` taken at line 102/107. The new record's (size, mtime) now match the file, so line 67 accepts it on every subsequent `facts()` call: the laundered staleness is permanent. `facts` will then return a high-water that is too low (a later append reuses a Lamport) and a `stamps` list whose payloads (e.g. `skew.overridden`, `ddflow.capabilities`) are the pre-rewrite values fed to the version guard. The same-size/rewrite case is exactly what the `mtime_ns` half of `_current`'s check exists to catch, and `advance` bypasses it.
title: ddflow/infra/shardmeta.py:103 (ShardMeta.advance)

detail: With evidence moved out of line, `LB.full(...)` substitutes `B.Unavailable` for `chunk_findings` whenever the referenced blob cannot be read, and this branch answers with a triage summary built from the same count keys the normal path returns (`findings`, `refuted`, `confirmed`, `untriaged`) — but it sets `"findings": 0` together with `"untriaged": 1`. That state is self-contradictory: one item is declared untriaged while the findings tally is zero, so any consumer that derives the settled count (`findings - untriaged`, or checks `findings >= untriaged`) sees -1 / a broken invariant, and the unreadable finding is simultaneously dropped from the tally instead of being surfaced. Concretely, take a log whose `gate.failed`/`gate.passed` event carries its `chunk_findings` as a blob reference and whose `.ddflow/blobs/<hash>.json` is missing (the blob was never committed, was deleted, or the shard was committed while the blob was still unwritten — hunk 1 bypasses the `whole()` completeness check for blobs, so this is reachable): running `ddflow status` on that clone reaches this line and reports zero findings plus one untriaged, where the count of findings that could not be read is exactly what the `unavailable`/`untriaged` signal is supposed to convey. Additionally, because this helper's contract is "return the triage to carry over, or `None` when the findings cannot be matched", returning a non-`None` summary here sends the caller down the carry-over path with an all-zero verdict set rather than the no-carry-over path the accompanying comment ("findings nobody can be said to have settled") describes.
title: ddflow/services/gates/outcomes.py (the `isinstance(found, B.Unavailable)` early return)

detail: `_append_lease_event` uses a single boolean for two different outcomes: "an event was appended" (the old contract, and what every caller checks as `ok`) and "the lease is still held but nothing was written". On the suppression path it returns `True` before `log.append(kind, item_id, payload(it.lease))` runs, so the caller in the renew path executes its `if ok:` branch as if a `lease.renewed` event had been committed, while the only durable record of the new expiry — the `{"at": ..., "holder": ...}` event the fold reads — is never written. The folded expiry is therefore frozen at the last *logged* renewal, and it can lag the real expiry by up to the coalescing window (`renew_window(Config.load(log.root))`, i.e. `[lease].renew_log_min_s`). Concrete input: ttl 300 s, `[lease].renew_log_min_s = 45`, `[lease].grace_s = 30`, holder heartbeating every 5 s. The claim is logged at t=0 (logged expiry 300); heartbeats at t=5..40 are suppressed because the extension stays ≤ 45 s, so the log-derived expiry is still 300 while the holder is alive. A second clone (or an old-skew ddflow reading the new log, per the skew guard) folds the same log, sees `expires_at - now < 0 - grace_s` and treats the lease as lapsed; its `lapsed_onto_a_live_claim`/takeover path can then take a live claim. The same staleness also feeds `core/handlers/leases.py::_late_renewal`, whose widening window is derived from the last renewal event, so coalescing shrinks that window too. Nothing in the diff bounds the suppression by `grace_s` or records the suppressed heartbeat anywhere (the `.ddflow/local` LocalStore fallback the intent mentions does not appear in this hunk), so the reorganisation-audit requirement "the expiry another clone computes is unchanged within grace_s" is not established at this site; the guard against `renew_log_min_s > grace_s` (config validation or clamping) is absent from the code under review. If that equality is enforced elsewhere (e.g. inside `logcoalesce.renew_window`), this is a

detail: The module docstring states the public entry point is `full(root, evidence)`, but the actual signature is `full(evidence, root=None)`. A caller written to the documented contract (`full(root, event["evidence"])`) gets back the `Path`, not the resolved evidence: the first parameter is then not a `dict`, so line `if not isinstance(evidence, dict) ...: return evidence` short-circuits and returns the path object unchanged, silently (no exception) handing a `Path` to code that expects an evidence mapping. Either the docstring or the parameter order is wrong; as written they disagree.
title: ddflow/services/logblobs.py:2 (module docstring) vs `full` at ~line 34

detail: With `root=None` the resolver walks every known project and keeps only the *last* store's verdict. Given a log in project A whose blob has been tampered with (so `fetch` returns `Unavailable(ref, "does not match its address (altered)")`) and any later store in `known_roots()` that simply lacks the ref, the loop overwrites `got` with `Unavailable(ref, "is missing from .ddflow/blobs")` and returns that. So in the fallback path an altered blob is reported as merely missing, losing exactly the tamper signal the module promises to surface; only the `root=`-pinned path (and `problems`) preserves the "altered" reason.
title: ddflow/services/logblobs.py:`full.get` (the `for store in stores` loop)

detail: `renew_window` clamps the coalescing window to `heartbeat_s` but never to `grace_s`, even though the module docstring's whole soundness argument is "the window adds to a delay it already tolerates, **inside `grace_s`**" and the reorganisation audit states the coalesced log is allowed only if the expiry another clone computes stays unchanged *within `grace_s`*. The two knobs are independent operator config, so the window can exceed `grace_s`. Concrete input: `[lease] renew_log_min_s = 600, heartbeat_s = 300, grace_s = 30`, a lease held with a renewal written at `t0`. `quiet_renewal` returns True (no event) for every heartbeat at `t0+300` because `age = 300 < min(600, 300)` — wait, `age == min_s` is not `<`, but for any renewal sequence denser than `heartbeat_s` (e.g. one renewal per command, which is exactly the workload that produced 46% `lease.renewed`), the last *written* renewal lags the true one by up to 300 s. With `grace_s = 30` that lag is outside the tolerance the docstring relies on: a second clone reading the log computes an expiry up to 270 s before the holder does (and if the local heartbeat is kept in `.ddflow/local` per the intent, the holder still believes it is alive), so it can acquire a lease the first holder still holds. Nothing in this file or in `renew_window` enforces `window <= grace_s`; if the bound lives in config validation it is not visible here and is not exercised by these functions.
title: ddflow/services/logcoalesce.py:22 (`renew_window`) / :28 (`quiet_renewal`)

detail: The coalescing rule drops the *newest* renewal of a run, not an intermediate one: `if key in last and 0 <= at - last[key] < min_s: continue` skips every renewal within `min_s` of the last *written* one, including the last one before the holder stops or before the tail ends. That means the event that would move the folded `renewed_at` forward is removed. Example: renewals at `t=0` and `t=10` with `min_s=60` — `last[L]=0`, `10-0 < 60` → the `t=10` event is dropped, so the folded `renewed_at` (and therefore the folded lease expiry shown by `status`/`board`) is `0 + duration` instead of `10 + duration`. The code's own docstring concedes this ("changes nothing but how recent the newest WRITTEN one is, by less than the window"), but the stated acceptance is "byte-identical fold output on this log" and "fold of the old log == fold of the coalesced/blob log for status, next, board, lease expiry" — those cannot both hold for any `min_s > 0`, and `coalesced` is precisely the function the replay-equivalence test would use to build the coalesced log. Either the acceptance/replay-equivalence test must compare something other than folded lease expiry, or the rule must retain the last renewal of every run (which cannot be decided without lookahead).
title: ddflow/services/logcoalesce.py:43-59 (`coalesced`)

detail: The fixture is the workload behind the "size/time ratchet test on a generated 10x log" and behind the acceptance metric "`lease.renewed` share under 10% of events", and its own module docstring claims it reproduces the real log's mix ("lease renewals are ~43% of events"; the research record says the real log is 46%). With the defaults (`beats=20`, `coalesce_s=0`) it does not: per item the writer emits 21 `lease.renewed` (1 initial + 20 in the beat loop) against only ~17 other events (`task.added`, `lease.acquired`, `item.started`, ~5×`gate.started` + 5×`gate.passed/failed`, ~2 `review.triaged`, `lease.released`, `item.completed`), i.e. ~55% renewals. This is not a knob artifact — the number of gates scales at `beats/2`, so the renewal share stays around 50-58% for any `beats` and tends to ~2/3 as `beats` grows; the gap comes from the fixture generating only ~17 non-renewal events per item where the real log has ~29 (53,163 events minus 24,413 renewals over ~1k items). So a call like `generate(tmp, 50_000)` produces a log whose `lease.renewed` fraction is ~53-58%, not the ~43%/46% it claims to model, and every before/after number derived from it (fold time, bytes, and the "<10%" share check) is measured on a workload that over-weights the very event kind the task is trying to remove, inflating the measured benefit of coalescing.
title: ddflow/services/logfixture.py:generate

detail: The record is internally contradictory and mis-classifies a log-format change as backward compatible. `impact = "additive"` states that an older release can still consume a log carrying this change, while the same record's `why` states the opposite: "an older ddflow is refused the gate events of such a log." This knob flips on a new on-disk event payload (`log.evidence_blobs = true` by default, with `log.evidence_blob_keys`/`min_bytes` deciding when a value becomes a content-addressed reference): a pre-change binary folding such an event sees the blob reference where it expects `tail`/`selected_tests`/`chunk_findings` and computes different gate evidence (or errors), and the review service's guard in `services/review.py` shows the new code already expects un-hydratable evidence to be surfaced rather than silently consumed. The operator requirement is explicit that "old ddflow refuses or reads the new log per the skew guard", so a change that changes what is written must not be filed `additive`; any tooling that keys the skew guard / upgrade plan off `impact` will not arm the guard, and a mixed-version or rolled-back clone will fold the same log to a different state instead of being refused. The correct classification for this one knob is the non-additive/breaking class (contrast the other three unreleased templates, whose knobs only add config and never change the encoded event payload).
title: ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.log.evidence_blobs.toml:8

detail:
The doc states that coalescing "is acknowledged and not recorded" and that the only cost is that "another clone sees the expiry up to that window early, inside `ttl_s` and `grace_s`." Nothing in the described design bounds the drift by `grace_s`: the bullet itself says the window is `renew_log_min_s`, "never more than `heartbeat_s`". So the permitted drift is `min(renew_log_min_s, heartbeat_s)`, which is unrelated to `grace_s`. Demonstrating input: a clone configured with `heartbeat_s = 60`, `renew_log_min_s = 30`, `grace_s = 10`. Clone A heartbeats every 30 s; every renewal is dropped, so the last written renewal stays 30 s stale. Clone B folds the log, computes `last_written_renewal + ttl_s`, and sees the lease as expired up to 30 s early — 3× `grace_s`. B then claims a lease A still holds. The reorganisation-audit caution for this item required the expiry another clone computes to be unchanged *within grace_s*, proven by a two-clone test; the doc instead asserts `grace_s` compliance with no invariant tying `renew_log_min_s ≤ grace_s` (or any clamp), so the asserted bound does not hold for admissible config.

The same bullet also understates the affected surface: `core/handlers/leases.py::_late_renewal` derives the widened lease window from the last renewal, so dropping renewals does not merely move "the expiry" — it changes the pairwise window the handler computes on another clone, again by up to the coalescing window without reference to `grace_s`. Describing the cost as "another clone sees the expiry up to that window early, inside `ttl_s` and `grace_s`" therefore misstates the observable change in the exact code path the audit flagged.
title: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md — "Log scale", renewals bullet

detail: `timed()` discards the child's exit status and captures its output, so a command that crashes still yields a plausible-looking `wall_s`/`cpu_s` line. This is not hypothetical for the `COMMANDS` tuple: `heartbeat B-synth-1` names an item that only exists in the synthetic fixture generated by `logfixture.generate`. Run the documented `logbench.py --events .ddflow/events` path (the "this log" measurement the acceptance table requires) and `ddflow heartbeat B-synth-1` has no such item, exits non-zero, and prints an error to the captured stderr — yet the harness emits `{"command": "heartbeat B-synth-1", "wall_s": ..., "cpu_s": ...}` as if the read path had executed. The same applies to any other invocation that errors under the stripped environment (`env` omits `LANG`/`XDG_*` and only sets `PYTHONPATH`, `PATH`, `HOME`): the before/after table would silently compare timings of failing runs, with no marker distinguishing them from successful ones. The script should at minimum record the return code (or use `check=True`) so a failed command is visible in the JSON output rather than reported as a measurement.
title: `scripts/logbench.py` `timed()` (the `subprocess.run(argv, cwd=cwd, env=env, capture_output=True, check=False)` call, ~line 48)

detail: `_folds` counts constructions of `records.State`, and `_run` runs `main(...)` inside `contextlib.suppress(SystemExit)`, so a command that exits early (argparse rejection, `sys.exit(1)` on error) is silently tolerated. `test_brief_folds_at_most_twice` then asserts `_folds(...) <= 2`, and `0 <= 2` is true, so a regression in which `brief` bails out before folding at all — the exact "fold once per command" property the intent requires and that the sibling test pins with `== 1` for `status`/`next` — makes this test pass vacuously: `n["folds"]` stays 0 and no assertion looks at the command's output. Concretely, if `brief` raises `SystemExit(1)` (or is refactored to read a fully up-to-date checkpoint and fold nothing), `_folds` returns 0 and the test still passes, while an implementation that folded 0 times because it failed would go undetected. A lower bound (e.g. `1 <= _folds(...) <= 2`) or an assertion on the produced output is needed for the test to guard what its docstring claims.
title: tests/test_fold_once.py test_brief_folds_at_most_twice

detail: The task's ACCEPTANCE says "lease.renewed share under 10% of events on the generated workload", and this test is named for that bound, but the body asserts `share < 0.25` (and only "5x fewer renewals than written"). The criterion the change commits to is therefore not pinned: a coalescing regression that leaves lease.renewed at, say, 24% of events (i.e. the acceptance target missed by 2.4x) still passes the suite. Given the whole point of step (2) is "lease.renewed share under 10%", the assertion should be `< 0.1` (or the acceptance text and test name should be corrected to match 25%). This is a concrete input — generated workload `logfixture.generate(..., 20000, seed=1, beat_gap_s=20.0, beats=60)` yielding a coalesced share between 0.1 and 0.25 — under which the change fails its acceptance while the tests stay green.
title: tests/test_log_scale.py::test_renewal_share_of_a_busy_workload_falls_under_ten_percent

detail: The acceptance and HOW-TO-TEST require the replay-equivalence proof to run "on this repository's real log copied into a tmp dir". These tests instead gate the real-log arm on `if (real / ".ddflow" / "events").is_dir(): logs.append(EventLog(real))`, reading the working tree in place (not copied) and silently omitting the arm when absent. On a clean checkout / CI (`git clone` without a `.ddflow/events` directory) each of these tests exercises only the generated fixture and passes with no skip or failure marker, so the real-log equivalence that the change is justified by is never actually verified there — yet the suite reports success. Any fixture that folds identically but diverges on the repo's real log (e.g. one containing the contested-claim/attachment shapes the generated fixture does not emit) would be missed. Additionally, using the developer's live log makes the result depend on the local working tree rather than a pinned copy, so the assertions are non-deterministic across machines.
title: tests/test_log_scale.py::test_fold_is_byte_identical_to_the_asdict_claim_on_a_contested_log / test_the_renewal_fast_path_folds_identically_to_the_full_window_logic / test_tasks_below_a_phase_equal_the_full_scan_in_the_same_order
